chain.g: to track; to hunt; to follow

ety.text: From Middle English wrek, from Anglo-Norman wrek, from Old Norse *wrek (whence Norwegian rek, Icelandic rek, Swedish vrak, Danish vrag), from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną (“to pursue”, whence Old English wrecan (English wreak), Old Saxon wrekan, Old High German rëhhan, Gothic 𐍅𐍂𐌹𐌺𐌰𐌽 (wrikan)), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to track; to hunt; to follow”).

senses.d: Something or someone that has been ruined.
ex: He was an emotional wreck after the death of his wife.

senses.d: The remains of something that has been severely damaged or worn down.
ex: To the fair haven of my native home, / The vvreck of vvhat I was, fatigued I come, […]
In 2006, 18-year-old Nikki Catsouras was killed in a car wreck in Lake Forest.

senses.d: An event in which something is damaged through collision.
ex: the wrecks of matter and the crush of worlds
Its intellectual life was thus able to go on amidst the wreck of its political life.

senses.d: A shipwreck: an event in which a ship is heavily damaged or destroyed.
Goods, etc. cast ashore by the sea after a shipwreck.
A large number of birds that have been brought to the ground, injured or dead, by extremely adverse weather.
ex: [I]n 1952 more than 7,000 were involved in such a "wreck" in Britain and Ireland.

senses.d: To destroy violently; to cause severe damage to something, to a point where it no longer works, or is useless.
ex: He wrecked the car in a collision.
That adulterous hussy wrecked my marriage!

senses.d: To ruin or dilapidate.
To plunder goods from wrecked ships.
To dismantle wrecked vehicles or other objects, to reclaim any useful parts.
To involve in a wreck; hence, to cause to suffer ruin; to balk of success, and bring disaster on.
ex: Weak and envy'd, if they should conspire, / They wreck themselves, and he hath his Desire.

senses.d: To be involved in a wreck; to be damaged or destroyed.

senses.d: Destroyed, usually in an accident; damaged to the point of unusability.
Very intoxicated from alcohol or recreational drugs.
Having been put in a dreadful or embarrassing situation; can range from being pwned in a game to being utterly defeated in an argument or publicly shamed with a stinging insult.

chain.g: to engage in grappling combat or sport, struggle, wrestle; to twist and turn, squirm, wriggle, writhe; (figurative) to contend, grapple with, struggle

ety.text: The verb is derived from Middle English wrestlen, wrastlen (“to engage in grappling combat or sport, struggle, wrestle; to twist and turn, squirm, wriggle, writhe; (figurative) to contend, grapple with, struggle”), from Old English wrǣstlian (“to wrestle”), a frequentative form of wrǣstan (“to twist, wrest”), from Proto-Germanic *wraistijaną (“to turn; to twist, wrest”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wreyt- (“to twist”). By surface analysis, wrest + -le (frequentative suffix). Probably related to wraxle (UK, dialectal, archaic). The noun is derived from the verb.

senses.d: To take part in (a wrestling bout or match).
ex: Hark thee, friend, […] wilt thou wrestle a fall with me?
Have we not wrestled a turn before now?

senses.d: Sometimes followed by down: to contend with or move (someone) into or out of a position by grappling; also, to overcome (someone) by grappling.
ex: My driver at the second station was a stout girl of twenty, strong enough to wrestle any man, but shy, modest, and gentle.

senses.d: To move or manipulate (something) using physical effort, usually with some difficulty or opposition.
ex: I couldn't wrestle the trunk down the hall.
And, wrestling both his arms into a gown, / He paused and took a survey up and down.

senses.d: To engage in (a contest or struggle).
To throw down (a calf or other livestock animal) for branding.
To grapple or otherwise contend with an opponent in order to throw or force them to the ground, chiefly as a sport or in unarmed combat.
ex: Wreſtell nat with me for I wyll throwe the [thee] on thy backe […]
[Y]ee gaue their diligẽce [diligence] to lerne to fight, to wriſtle, to leape, to daunce, ⁊ to put at yͤ ſtone: […]

senses.d: Followed by with: to move or manipulate something using physical effort, usually with some difficulty or opposition.
ex: It fits Ioues ſonne / VVraſtle vvith Lyons, and to tugge vvith Beares, / Grapple vvith Dragons, and incounter VVhales.
I've spent this whole morning rassling with that dumb horse, Sam …

senses.d: To make one's way or move with some difficulty or effort.
Followed by against or with: to contend, to struggle; to exert effort, to strive.
ex: And thus go theſe Prelates about to vvreſtle for honour, that it may be reported abroad, that vve breed hereſies againſt ourſelves.
[T]hey their ſhips in marble ſeas with ores dyd wraſtlyng towe.

senses.d: To contend verbally; to argue, to debate, to dispute.
A fight or struggle between people during which they grapple or otherwise contend with each other in order to throw or force their opponent to the ground, chiefly as a sport or in unarmed combat.
ex: Beyond the tilt-yard spread the larger space, / For the strong wrestle and the breathless race; […]

senses.d: A situation in which people compete with each other; a contest, a struggle.
The action of contending or struggling.
ex: War in Italy, universal spasm of wrestle there, being now the expectation of foolish mankind.
